messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Malia, a 61-year-old security guard of Oceania descent, lives alone in a small apartment outside Portland. She has worked the night shift at a downtown office building for nearly two decades, a job that once gave her a quiet sense of purpose. That changed eighteen months ago, when she was making her rounds through the underground parking garage and came upon a young man trying to jimmy open a car door. She shouted, he spun around, and in the confusion of the dim light and the echoing concrete, she swung her flashlight at him. It connected with his temple. He crumpled to the ground, and she saw blood pooling beneath his head. She called 911, but by the time the paramedics arrived, he was unresponsive. He survived, but with lasting brain damage. Malia has not worked a shift since.

What haunts her most is the blank space in her memory. There are parts of the event she simply cannot retrieve—the exact moment before she swung, the sound he made, the way his body fell. She will sit on her couch, staring at the wall, trying to force the images back, but they refuse to come. Instead, what she recalls feels like it belongs to someone else, a stranger in a uniform she no longer recognizes. Sometimes she can replay the scene in her head but feels nothing at all—a hollow, emotionless replay, as if she is watching a film of a woman who is not her. It is this emotional flatness that frightens her most, because she knows she should feel something, and the absence of feeling convinces her that she is a monster.

Because the memory feels alien and incomplete, Malia has become obsessed with filling in the gaps. She dwells on what she did wrong—why she swung so hard, why she did not just use her voice, why she did not see that he was just a frightened kid. She goes over and over the details of those few seconds, trying to reconstruct them, trying to make sense of how a routine patrol turned into a life-altering mistake. She thinks constantly about why the event has happened to her, as if finding an answer might undo it. But the more she analyzes, the more fragmented the memory becomes. The gaps widen. The story feels less like her own. Her obsessive rumination does not clarify the past; it drives the memory further away, making it feel even more alien, more like something that happened to a stranger. She will spend an entire evening turning the same few seconds over in her mind, and by morning she is less certain of what really happened than she was the night before.

This cycle has hollowed out her life. She has not returned to the parking garage, and she cannot imagine ever working security again. She avoids the downtown area entirely, taking the long bus route to the grocery store. Her daughter, who lives two hours away, calls every Sunday, but Malia keeps the conversations short. She has come to believe that if anyone knew what she had done, they would see her the way she sees herself: as someone dangerous, someone who should not be trusted. She has stopped answering texts from her few remaining friends. The isolation felt like protection at first, but now it is just a quiet, empty room.

What finally brought her to a clinic was a panic attack in the security aisle of a hardware store. She had gone to buy a new lock for her front door, and the sight of a row of heavy-duty flashlights sent her heart racing. She left the cart where it was and walked out. That night, she called her daughter and admitted she could not keep going like this. She is afraid of what she might find out in therapy—that she is irredeemable, that the blank spaces in her memory are hiding something even worse. But she is more afraid of spending the rest of her years alone in that apartment, replaying a moment she cannot fully remember and cannot forgive.
